stops.name: Maipú, El Abrazo de Maipú
stops.campa: The companion canvas to Chacabuco, also acquired by Argentina in 1908: O'Higgins, arm in a sling, thrown against San Martín's neck before the smoke has cleared from the plain of Maipú, the two liberators fused into the single embrace both nations still repeat at every anniversary. Subercaseaux paints the gesture larger than the battle around it: the point of the whole campaign reduced to two men holding on to each other. The canvas is pinned here to the identical field where both O'Higgins's and San Martín's own itineraries place their abrazo: the same afternoon, seen once from inside it and once from an easel.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El Cabildo Abierto del 22 de Mayo de 1810
stops.campa: Commissioned by the Argentine historian Ángel Justiniano Carranza for the Centenary, Subercaseaux builds a cardboard maqueta of the old Cabildo's upper floor and works from photographs Carranza sends him of the room and of portraits of the men who sat in it, reconstructing 22 May 1810 stroke by careful stroke from a Santiago studio. The canvas becomes the picture Argentina still teaches its children: Castelli mid-oration, Belgrano among the sworn vecinos below the arches. In this atlas the meta-pin is exact: the painter's stop and Belgrano's stop share the same plaza, the same square meter of history, forty years apart.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, second place, the Centennial Competition
stops.campa: For the Centenario itself, May 1910, Buenos Aires holds an international competition of historical painting; Subercaseaux, already the man Argentina has trusted with its Cabildo and its Chacabuco, takes second place among painters from across the hemisphere. He is thirty years old, a Chilean judged among the best history painters of two republics on the exact day both nations toast their independence: the decade's honors converging on a single week in a single city that is not, technically, his own, though by now it might as well be.

stops.name: Vatican City, the portrait of Pope Pius X
stops.campa: In 1911 the Holy See commissions Subercaseaux to paint Pius X from life; he sits before the pontiff in Rome, dressed in the tailcoat protocol demands, and delivers a canvas that is hung in the Vatican's Gallery of the Popes: the only work by a South American painter ever given that place. He signs it as the layman he still is: married, elegant, painting popes and generals with the same even hand. Neither he nor the Pope can know that the painter will return to this same canvas forty-three years later, in a different habit, to finish it a second time.

stops.name: Santiago, El Descubrimiento de Chile, the Salón de Honor
stops.campa: At the request of the presidents of both chambers, Subercaseaux paints his largest Chilean commission: Diego de Almagro's column sighting the Aconcagua valley in 1536, the Discovery raised to fill the Salón de Honor of the National Congress. The mural draws immediate fire from specialists over its botany, its stars, its ethnography, a controversy the painter later weighs in his memoirs, left thoughtful that every objection touched some particular detail and not one touched the composition as a whole. It still hangs there, restored in 2023, the single largest canvas the decade of centennials leaves behind him.
stops.quote: Las críticas se referían todas a detalles particulares del cuadro. No hubo ni una sola observación al conjunto de la composición, ni sobre sus méritos o deméritos en cuanto obra de arte, lo que me dejó pensativo.

stops.name: Assisi, the life of the Poverello
stops.campa: Between commissions for generals and popes, Subercaseaux begins the studies that will become his watercolor life of Saint Francis, walking the same Umbrian hill-town streets the saint walked, sketching the basilica's frescoes for their own instruction in how a life is told through images alone. The Conquest and the Independence had drawn him, he says, for heroism and the picturesque together; here he finds a third register he has not yet named, sanctity, and the historical painter, without quite noticing the hinge turn under his feet, begins learning to paint a different kind of glory.

stops.name: Santiago, the war years, the vocation ripens
stops.campa: Europe burns through the Great War while Chile stays neutral and Subercaseaux keeps painting, but something in the household is already turning. He and Elvira have spoken of a fuller religious life abstractly, he will later write, for several years before the idea takes its final shape; the war's scale of dying seems to press the question rather than create it. Fourteen years of marriage lie behind them, decades of easels and diplomatic drawing-rooms; ahead, though neither says the word aloud yet, lies the ecclesiastical door his own school days at Douai first opened without his knowing it.

stops.name: Rome, the audience with Benedict XV
stops.campa: Pedro and Elvira sail for Rome together to ask, in person, an audience of Pope Benedict XV: two married aristocrats kneeling before the Holy See to request the rarest of graces, the dissolution of a good marriage so that both parties may take religious vows. The pope receives them and grants it. The canon savors the inversion: most petitioners come to Rome to be married, to be annulled of a failure, or to be absolved; these two come asking permission to succeed at something harder, and leave the audience still husband and wife and already parted in everything but the road.

stops.name: Loyola, the parting without tears
stops.campa: The parting itself happens in Spain, at the sanctuary raised over the birthplace of Saint Ignatius, on the feast of the Assumption: after thirteen years of marriage, Pedro and Elvira separate by mutual and entirely free decision to enter religious life apart. Subercaseaux records the scene himself, insisting on its peace against every expectation of grief: no tears, no sobs, no discomposed gesture, only an interior calm that seemed, he writes, a reflection of the mountains' soft blue. He genuflects before the Blessed Sacrament, turns, and walks out without looking back, carrying her parting gift: a holy card with her photograph and a prayer on the back.
stops.quote: No hubo en todo aquello ni lágrimas, ni sollozos, ni un ademán desacompasado. Hubo paz y alegría interior que parecía reflejo del suave azul de las montañas.

stops.name: Loyola, Elvira enters the Damas Catequistas
stops.campa: Elvira stays where the parting leaves her: the same day she enters the novitiate of the Damas Catequistas at Loyola, taking up the teaching and catechizing life of the congregation the Venerable Dolores Sopeña built for the working poor of Spain's cities. The marriage the canon kept bright at its wedding day now ends exactly as both partners chose it to: not estranged but doubled, one vocation splitting cleanly into two, each spouse walking now toward a different enclosure on a different sea. Her path leaves the Chilean historical record here, a name folded into a Spanish congregation's own quieter chronicle.

stops.name: Quarr Abbey, Isle of Wight, a choir postulant
stops.campa: Pedro crosses to England and enters the Benedictine house of Our Lady of Quarr on the Isle of Wight as a postulant of the choir, forty years old, trading the tailcoat of the Vatican sitting for a habit sewn to no protocol at all. He will confess later that the old life does not release him easily: night after night, in dreams, he is still traveling: trains and steamers, hotels and passports, the itinerant painter's whole vocabulary of movement surfacing under the stability he has chosen and will swear solemnly in 1923. The cloister and the wanderer negotiate for years before the second one yields.
stops.quote: ...noche tras noche, en viajes en trenes y en vapores, en hoteles y pasaportes...

stops.name: Quarr, the watercolors of Saint Francis, published in Boston
stops.campa: The Assisi studies of a decade earlier ripen, inside the enclosure, into a full watercolor cycle of the life of Saint Francis; the Marshall Jones Company of Boston publishes the series in 1925 with text by the Danish convert-poet Johannes Jørgensen, and it is received abroad with real acclaim. The historical painter's old grammar, legible gesture, readable event, a scene built to carry its whole story at a glance, turns out to serve hagiography exactly as well as it served battle. Quarr's postulant is, without leaving the choir stalls, still an internationally exhibited artist.
